notes: Reasoning Ability part of BATCH_002: 200 original questions (60 Basic, 80 Intermediate, 60 Advanced) built by tools/batch_002/reasoning.py. New puzzle structures (vacant seats, unknown row length, two rows facing the same way, concentric circles, rectangular table, flats with vacancies, two stacks, unknown stack size, box weights, numeric ages on floors, calendar dates, joining years). Puzzles are brute-forced for a unique arrangement; syllogisms are checked over every Venn-region model; inequalities over all integer assignments; data sufficiency by enumerating models for each statement subset; blood relations, directions, coding, series, alphabet, ranking and input-output are recomputed in code. Verbal-reasoning items are hand-written and re-checked. All questions await human review.

stimuli.title: Seven persons in a row facing south
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Aman, Bhoomi, Chirayu, Dhara, Eklavya, Gunjan and Hitesh sit in a straight row, all facing south. (For a person facing south, the right is towards the west and the left is towards the east.)

- Hitesh sits at one of the extreme ends of the row.
- Only two persons sit between Hitesh and Aman.
- Gunjan sits immediately to the right of Aman.
- Dhara sits third to the left of Gunjan.
- Chirayu is an immediate neighbour of Hitesh.
- Bhoomi sits immediately to the left of Aman.
stimuli.solution:
Hitesh is at an end and Aman is three seats from him. Gunjan is immediately to Aman's right (west) and Dhara third to Gunjan's left (east), so Dhara is two seats east of Aman. If Hitesh were at the east end (seat 7 from the west), Aman = 4, Gunjan = 3 and Dhara = 6, and Chirayu, Hitesh's neighbour, would need seat 6: rejected. So Hitesh is at the west end (seat 1), Aman = 4, Gunjan = 3, Dhara = 6, Chirayu = 2, Bhoomi (immediately to Aman's left, i.e. east) = 5 and Eklavya = 7.

| Seat (west to east) | Person |
|---|---|
| 1 | Hitesh |
| 2 | Chirayu |
| 3 | Gunjan |
| 4 | Aman |
| 5 | Bhoomi |
| 6 | Dhara |
| 7 | Eklavya |

stimuli.title: Six persons in a row of nine seats
stimuli.content:
A row has nine seats, numbered 1 to 9 from the left end. Six persons Jignesh, Kritika, Manan, Nupur, Parth and Rachna sit in six of the seats, all facing north; the other three seats are vacant.

- Kritika sits at the extreme left end of the row.
- Exactly one seat lies between Kritika and Parth, and that seat is vacant.
- Manan sits immediately to the right of Parth.
- Jignesh sits third to the right of Nupur.
- Rachna sits second to the left of Jignesh.
- The seat immediately to the right of Rachna is vacant.
- Neither of the two end seats of the row is vacant.
stimuli.solution:
Kritika = 1, seat 2 is vacant, Parth = 3 and Manan = 4. Rachna is second to the left of Jignesh and Jignesh third to the right of Nupur, so Nupur, Rachna and Jignesh sit at n, n + 1 and n + 3. Seat 9 must be occupied, and only these three persons are left, so Jignesh = 9, Rachna = 7 and Nupur = 6. Seat 8 (to Rachna's right) and seat 5 are vacant.

| Seat | Occupant |
|---|---|
| 1 | Kritika |
| 2 | vacant |
| 3 | Parth |
| 4 | Manan |
| 5 | vacant |
| 6 | Nupur |
| 7 | Rachna |
| 8 | vacant |
| 9 | Jignesh |

stimuli.title: A row of unknown length
stimuli.content:
Some persons sit in a straight row, all facing north. The number of persons in the row is not given. Aarti, Bharat, Chhavi, Dinesh, Eshita, Faisal, Girija and Hemant are among them.

- Dinesh sits sixth from the left end of the row.
- Only two persons sit between Dinesh and Eshita.
- Faisal sits fourth to the left of Eshita.
- Aarti sits second to the left of Faisal.
- Bharat sits third to the right of Eshita.
- As many persons sit between Aarti and Bharat as between Bharat and Hemant.
- Hemant sits at one of the extreme ends of the row.
- Girija sits exactly in the middle of the row.
- Only five persons sit between Girija and Chhavi.
stimuli.solution:
Count positions from the left end. Dinesh = 6, so Eshita = 3 or 9. Faisal is four places to Eshita's left, which is impossible from 3, so Eshita = 9, Faisal = 5, Aarti = 3 and Bharat = 12. Eight persons sit between Aarti and Bharat, so Hemant is nine places from Bharat: 3 (Aarti's seat) or 21. Hence Hemant = 21, and as he is at an end, the row has 21 persons. The middle of 21 is 11 (Girija). Chhavi is six places from Girija: 5 (Faisal's seat) or 17, so Chhavi = 17.

| Position from the left | Person |
|---|---|
| 3 | Aarti |
| 5 | Faisal |
| 6 | Dinesh |
| 9 | Eshita |
| 11 | Girija |
| 12 | Bharat |
| 17 | Chhavi |
| 21 | Hemant |

All other positions are held by persons whose names are not given.

stimuli.title: Two rows facing the same way
stimuli.content:
Ten persons Aditya, Bela, Chetna, Darshan, Esha, Gopal, Indu, Jatin, Kirti and Lalit sit in two parallel rows of five seats each. All of them face north. Row 1 is in front (to the north) and Row 2 is directly behind it, so each person in Row 2 sits directly behind one person of Row 1. Who sits in which row is not given.

- Aditya sits in the middle of one of the rows.
- The person who sits directly in front of Aditya sits immediately to the right of Indu.
- Chetna sits directly behind Kirti.
- Kirti is an immediate neighbour of Darshan.
- Gopal and Bela sit at the two extreme ends of the same row.
- Lalit sits immediately to the right of Chetna.
- Esha sits second to the left of Chetna.
- Jatin does not sit directly behind Gopal.
stimuli.solution:
Someone sits in front of Aditya, so Aditya is in the middle of Row 2, and the person in front of him (Row 1, seat 3) is immediately to the right of Indu: Indu is at Row 1, seat 2. Chetna sits behind Kirti, so Kirti is in Row 1 and Chetna in Row 2. Chetna has Lalit on her right and Esha second to her left, so Chetna is at seat 3 or 4 of Row 2; seat 3 is Aditya's, so Chetna = Row 2 seat 4, Esha = seat 2, Lalit = seat 5, and Kirti = Row 1 seat 4. Darshan is next to Kirti: Row 1 seat 3 or 5. Gopal and Bela must be at both ends of one row; Row 2 already has Lalit at an end, so they take Row 1 seats 1 and 5, which puts Darshan at Row 1 seat 3. Jatin takes Row 2 seat 1; he is not behind Gopal, so Bela = Row 1 seat 1 and Gopal = Row 1 seat 5.

| Seat (west to east) | Row 1 (front) | Row 2 (behind) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Bela | Jatin |
| 2 | Indu | Esha |
| 3 | Darshan | Aditya |
| 4 | Kirti | Chetna |
| 5 | Gopal | Lalit |

stimuli.title: Seven persons and a vacant chair
stimuli.content:
Eight chairs are placed around a circular table, equally spaced. Seven persons Mahi, Nirav, Oshin, Prakash, Qadir, Rupa and Sagar sit on seven of them, all facing the centre; one chair is vacant. Positions such as 'second to the right' are counted by chairs, including the vacant chair.

- Mahi sits opposite Nirav.
- The vacant chair is second to the right of Mahi.
- Sagar sits immediately to the left of Nirav.
- Oshin sits second to the right of Sagar.
- Prakash sits immediately to the left of Mahi.
- Qadir does not sit next to the vacant chair.
stimuli.solution:
Fix Mahi. Nirav is opposite her (four chairs away), the vacant chair is second to her right and Prakash immediately to her left. Sagar is immediately to Nirav's left, i.e. between the vacant chair and Nirav, and Oshin is second to Sagar's right, i.e. immediately to Nirav's right. The two chairs left are the one between Mahi and the vacant chair and the one between Oshin and Prakash. Qadir cannot sit next to the vacant chair, so Qadir sits between Oshin and Prakash and Rupa between Mahi and the vacant chair.

| Chair (anticlockwise from Mahi) | Occupant |
|---|---|
| 0 | Mahi |
| 1 | Rupa |
| 2 | the vacant chair |
| 3 | Sagar |
| 4 | Nirav |
| 5 | Oshin |
| 6 | Qadir |
| 7 | Prakash |

stimuli.title: Seven persons around a circle, facing in or out
stimuli.content:
Seven persons Anirudh, Bindiya, Chandra, Deepak, Eshani, Firdaus and Gagan sit around a circular table, equally spaced. Some of them face the centre and the others face outside. (For a person facing the centre the right is anticlockwise; for a person facing outside the right is clockwise.)

- Anirudh faces the centre, and Chandra sits second to the right of Anirudh.
- Gagan sits between Anirudh and Chandra and faces outside.
- Firdaus is an immediate neighbour of Anirudh.
- Bindiya sits second to the right of Firdaus.
- Deepak sits immediately to the right of Bindiya.
- Chandra sits immediately to the right of Eshani.
- Exactly three persons face outside.
- Deepak and Chandra face the same direction.
stimuli.solution:
Fix Anirudh (facing the centre). Chandra is two seats anticlockwise from him and Gagan (facing outside) sits between them; Firdaus takes the seat on Anirudh's other side. If Firdaus faced the centre, second to his right would be Gagan's seat, so Firdaus faces outside and Bindiya sits two seats clockwise from him. The two seats left lie on either side of Bindiya. Chandra is immediately to Eshani's right, so Eshani is Chandra's neighbour (the seat between Chandra and Bindiya) and, to have Chandra on her right, faces outside. Deepak takes the seat between Bindiya and Firdaus; being immediately to Bindiya's right, he makes Bindiya face the centre. Gagan, Firdaus and Eshani are the three facing outside, so Chandra and Deepak face the centre.

| Anticlockwise from Anirudh | Person | Faces |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Anirudh | centre |
| 1 | Gagan | outside |
| 2 | Chandra | centre |
| 3 | Eshani | outside |
| 4 | Bindiya | centre |
| 5 | Deepak | centre |
| 6 | Firdaus | outside |

stimuli.title: Two concentric circles
stimuli.content:
Eight persons Harini, Ibrahim, Juhi, Kishore, Leena, Mridul, Nayan and Oindrila sit around two concentric circular tables, four at each, equally spaced. The persons at the inner table face outside, and those at the outer table face the centre, so every inner person faces exactly one outer person. Positions such as 'to the right' are counted among the persons of one's own circle.

- Harini sits in the outer circle and faces Nayan.
- Mridul sits second to the right of Harini.
- Leena faces Mridul.
- Juhi sits immediately to the right of Leena.
- Kishore faces Juhi.
- Ibrahim is an immediate neighbour of Nayan.
stimuli.solution:
Harini is in the outer circle facing Nayan (inner). Facing the centre, Harini's right is anticlockwise, so Mridul is the outer seat opposite Harini, and Leena (inner) faces Mridul. Leena faces outside, so her right is clockwise; the inner seat immediately clockwise of Leena is Juhi's, and Kishore is the outer person facing Juhi, i.e. immediately to Harini's right. Ibrahim must sit beside Nayan in the inner circle; the only free inner seat is the one opposite Juhi, so Ibrahim sits there, and Oindrila takes the last outer seat, facing Ibrahim.

| Place (anticlockwise) | Outer circle (faces centre) | Inner circle (faces outside) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Harini | Nayan |
| 2 | Kishore | Juhi |
| 3 | Mridul | Leena |
| 4 | Oindrila | Ibrahim |

stimuli.title: Nine flats on three floors
stimuli.content:
Nine persons Ankur, Barkha, Charan, Disha, Emon, Falak, Gaurang, Heer and Imtiaz live in a three-storey building, one in each flat. Floor 1 is the lowermost and floor 3 the topmost. Each floor has three flats in a line from west to east: West, Middle and East. Each flat is directly above the flat of the same name on the floor below.

- Imtiaz lives in a Middle flat, but not on the topmost floor.
- Ankur lives in the flat directly above Imtiaz's flat.
- Emon lives in the flat directly below Imtiaz's flat.
- Barkha lives in an East flat on the same floor as Imtiaz.
- Disha lives in the flat directly above Barkha's flat.
- Heer lives in the flat directly above Charan's flat, and both live in West flats.
- Falak lives in a West flat, on the same floor as Gaurang.
stimuli.solution:
Imtiaz has a flat above him (Ankur) and a flat below him (Emon), so Imtiaz must be in 2-Middle, Ankur in 3-Middle and Emon in 1-Middle. Barkha is in 2-East and Disha above her in 3-East. The West flats of all three floors and 1-East are left. Heer is directly above Charan in the West column, so they take 3-West/2-West or 2-West/1-West, and Falak takes the remaining West flat. Falak shares a floor with Gaurang, and the only non-West flat left is 1-East, so Falak = 1-West, Gaurang = 1-East, Charan = 2-West and Heer = 3-West.

| Floor | West | Middle | East |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | Heer | Ankur | Disha |
| 2 | Charan | Imtiaz | Barkha |
| 1 | Falak | Emon | Gaurang |

stimuli.title: Six floors and six ages
stimuli.content:
Six persons Jayesh, Kesar, Lohit, Madhu, Nitin and Pranali live on the six floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost). Their ages, in years, are 24, 27, 31, 35, 38 and 42, one age each.

- The person aged 42 lives on floor 2.
- Jayesh lives two floors above the person aged 42.
- Pranali lives immediately above Jayesh.
- The youngest person lives immediately below Jayesh.
- Jayesh is older than both the persons living above him.
- Lohit lives on the topmost floor and is older than Pranali.
- Madhu is 11 years younger than Kesar.
- Nitin lives above Madhu.
stimuli.solution:
The 42-year-old is on floor 2, Jayesh on 4, Pranali on 5 and the 24-year-old on 3; Lohit is on 6. So Kesar, Madhu and Nitin share floors 1, 2 and 3, where floor 2 holds age 42 and floor 3 age 24. Ages 11 apart are 24–35, 27–38 and 31–42. Madhu 24 (floor 3) is impossible because Nitin must live above Madhu; Madhu 27 with Kesar 38 is impossible because only floor 1 has an age other than 42 and 24. So Kesar is 42 (floor 2) and Madhu 31 on floor 1, leaving floor 3 (24) for Nitin. Floors 4, 5 and 6 share 27, 35 and 38 with Jayesh older than Lohit and Pranali, and Lohit older than Pranali: Jayesh 38, Lohit 35, Pranali 27.

| Floor | Person | Age |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Lohit | 35 |
| 5 | Pranali | 27 |
| 4 | Jayesh | 38 |
| 3 | Nitin | 24 |
| 2 | Kesar | 42 |
| 1 | Madhu | 31 |

stimuli.title: Eight persons in ten flats
stimuli.content:
A five-storey building has two flats on each floor: flat A to the west and flat B to the east, with each flat A directly above the flat A of the floor below (and likewise for B). Floor 1 is the lowermost. Eight persons Ritesh, Sneh, Tulika, Umang, Varsha, Wahid, Yashvi and Zoravar live in eight of the flats, one in each; two flats are vacant.

- Tulika lives in flat B of an odd-numbered floor, and flat A of her floor is vacant.
- Ritesh lives directly above Tulika.
- Umang lives on the same floor as Ritesh.
- Yashvi lives directly above Umang.
- The flat directly above Ritesh's flat is vacant.
- Sneh lives in flat B, two floors below Ritesh.
- Varsha lives in flat A on a floor below Zoravar's floor.
- Wahid lives on the lowermost floor.
stimuli.solution:
Tulika is in flat B of floor 1, 3 or 5. Floor 5 leaves no flat above her for Ritesh. Floor 1 puts Ritesh in 2-B, and Sneh would have to live two floors below floor 2: impossible. So Tulika = 3-B (3-A vacant), Ritesh = 4-B, 5-B vacant, Umang = 4-A, Yashvi = 5-A and Sneh = 2-B. That uses both vacant flats, so 1-A, 1-B and 2-A are occupied by Varsha, Wahid and Zoravar. Wahid is on floor 1; Varsha is in a flat A below Zoravar, so Varsha = 1-A, Zoravar = 2-A and Wahid = 1-B.

| Floor | Flat A (west) | Flat B (east) |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Yashvi | vacant |
| 4 | Umang | Ritesh |
| 3 | vacant | Tulika |
| 2 | Zoravar | Sneh |
| 1 | Varsha | Wahid |

stimuli.title: Six boxes in two stacks
stimuli.content:
Six boxes D, F, H, J, L and N are kept in two stacks, X (on the left) and Y (on the right), with three boxes in each stack. Level 1 is the bottom of a stack and level 3 its top.

- Box J is in stack X.
- Box D is placed directly above box J.
- Box H is at the top of the stack that does not contain box D.
- Box L is at the same level as box D, but in the other stack.
- Box F is placed below box L in the same stack.
- Box N is not at the bottom of either stack.
stimuli.solution:
Box J is in stack X with D directly above it, so J and D are at levels 1–2 or 2–3 of stack X. L sits at D's level in stack Y, and H is at the top of stack Y. If D were at level 3, L would also be at level 3 of Y, which is H's place. So J = X1, D = X2 and L = Y2. F is below L: Y1. N takes the remaining place, X3 (not a bottom place).

| Level | Stack X | Stack Y |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | N | H |
| 2 | D | L |
| 1 | J | F |

stimuli.title: Seven boxes and their weights
stimuli.content:
Seven boxes B, C, E, G, I, K and M are placed one above another in a single stack. Their weights are 10 kg, 14 kg, 17 kg, 21 kg, 25 kg, 28 kg and 32 kg, one weight per box.

- Box G is the heaviest box and is placed third from the bottom.
- Only two boxes are placed between box G and the lightest box.
- Box I is placed immediately above the lightest box and weighs 17 kg.
- Box K is placed at the bottom of the stack and weighs twice as much as box C.
- Box C is placed immediately above box K.
- Box E is placed immediately above box M, and E is heavier than M.
stimuli.solution:
G (32 kg) is third from the bottom, so the lightest box is three places from it: sixth from the bottom. I (17 kg) is seventh. K is at the bottom and C second. Among the weights left (10, 14, 21, 25, 28) the only pair where one is twice the other is 14 and 28, so K = 28 kg and C = 14 kg. E sits immediately above M, so they take places 4 and 5 (if they took 5 and 6, E would be the lightest, yet heavier than M). B takes place 6 and is the lightest (10 kg). E is heavier than M: E = 25, M = 21.

| Place from the bottom | Box | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | I | 17 kg |
| 6 | B | 10 kg |
| 5 | E | 25 kg |
| 4 | M | 21 kg |
| 3 | G | 32 kg |
| 2 | C | 14 kg |
| 1 | K | 28 kg |

stimuli.title: A stack of unknown size
stimuli.content:
Some boxes are placed one above another in a single stack. The number of boxes is not given. Boxes R, S, T, U, V, W, X and Y are among them; the other boxes are unnamed.

- Box T is placed fifth from the bottom.
- Only three boxes are placed between box T and box W.
- Box V is placed immediately below box W.
- As many boxes are placed above box W as below box T.
- Box R is placed exactly in the middle of the stack.
- Only two boxes are placed between box R and box S, and S is placed above V.
- Only one box is placed between box U and box S, and U is not at the top of the stack.
- Box X is at the top of the stack, and box Y is placed second from the bottom.
stimuli.solution:
Number places from the bottom. T = 5, so W = 9 or 1; V is immediately below W, so W = 9 and V = 8. Four boxes are below T, so four are above W: the stack has 9 + 4 = 13 boxes. R is in the middle, 7th. S is three places from R (4 or 10) and above V (8), so S = 10. U is two places from S (8 or 12); 8 is V's place, so U = 12, which is not the top. X = 13 and Y = 2.

| Place from the bottom | Box |
|---|---|
| 13 | X |
| 12 | U |
| 10 | S |
| 9 | W |
| 8 | V |
| 7 | R |
| 5 | T |
| 2 | Y |

The other places hold unnamed boxes.

stimuli.title: Seven trainings from March to September
stimuli.content:
Seven employees Akhil, Bhargavi, Chetas, Dipti, Ehsan, Firoza and Gautam attend a training programme, one in each month from March to September of the same year.

- Akhil's training is in a month that has 31 days.
- Chetas's training is in a month after Akhil's, and only one person's training is between theirs.
- Firoza's training is in the month immediately before Chetas's.
- Bhargavi's training is in the month immediately after Chetas's.
- Ehsan's training is in a month that has 30 days, after Bhargavi's.
- Gautam's training is in a month that has 30 days.
- Dipti's training is in a month before Gautam's.
stimuli.solution:
Akhil, Firoza, Chetas and Bhargavi take four consecutive months, with Akhil's month having 31 days, and Ehsan comes later in a 30-day month. Akhil in July or August leaves no room. Akhil in March gives Firoza April, Chetas May, Bhargavi June and Ehsan September; Dipti and Gautam would take July and August, but Gautam's month must have 30 days: rejected. So Akhil = May, Firoza = June, Chetas = July, Bhargavi = August, Ehsan = September, and Gautam (30 days, after Dipti) = April, Dipti = March.

| Month | Employee |
|---|---|
| March | Dipti |
| April | Gautam |
| May | Akhil |
| June | Firoza |
| July | Chetas |
| August | Bhargavi |
| September | Ehsan |

stimuli.title: Six visits on six dates of July
stimuli.content:
Six persons Harshad, Ishita, Jairaj, Kalyani, Lavesh and Meghna visit a bank branch on six different dates of July: the 3rd, 8th, 12th, 17th, 23rd and 28th. Each person visits once.

- Ishita visits on an odd-numbered date after the 12th.
- Only one person visits between Ishita and Jairaj.
- Lavesh visits on the date immediately after Ishita's (no one visits between them).
- Harshad visits on an even-numbered date, before Meghna.
- Kalyani visits before Harshad.
- Meghna visits on a date that is a multiple of 4, and before Jairaj.
stimuli.solution:
Ishita visits on the 17th or the 23rd, with Lavesh on the next date of the list. If Ishita = 23rd, Lavesh = 28th and Jairaj = 12th; Meghna must be before Jairaj on a multiple of 4, i.e. the 8th, and Harshad before her on an even date: impossible (only the 3rd is earlier). So Ishita = 17th and Lavesh = 23rd, and Jairaj, two dates away from Ishita, is on the 8th or the 28th. Meghna (a multiple of 4) must come before Jairaj, which rules out the 8th, so Jairaj = 28th. Kalyani, Harshad and Meghna take the 3rd, 8th and 12th in that order (Kalyani before Harshad before Meghna).

| Date (July) | Person |
|---|---|
| 3 | Kalyani |
| 8 | Harshad |
| 12 | Meghna |
| 17 | Ishita |
| 23 | Lavesh |
| 28 | Jairaj |

stimuli.title: Six birthdays in twelve months
stimuli.content:
Six friends Neeraj, Ovi, Pramod, Ruchi, Sumit and Tanisha were born in six different months of the same year (not a leap year). In each of the other six months none of them was born.

- Neeraj was born in a month that has 30 days.
- Tanisha was born in the month immediately after Neeraj's month.
- Pramod was born after Tanisha, and exactly two months lie between their months.
- Ovi was born after Pramod, and exactly one month lies between their months.
- Sumit was born in a month that has 31 days, after Ovi's month.
- Ruchi was born in the shortest month of the year.
stimuli.solution:
Neeraj's month has 30 days: April, June, September or November. Tanisha is the next month, Pramod three months after Tanisha and Ovi two months after Pramod. From September or November the chain runs past December. From June: Tanisha July, Pramod October, Ovi December, and Sumit (31 days, after Ovi) has no month left. So Neeraj = April, Tanisha = May, Pramod = August, Ovi = October and Sumit = December (the only 31-day month after October). Ruchi = February.

| Month | Born |
|---|---|
| January | — |
| February | Ruchi |
| March | — |
| April | Neeraj |
| May | Tanisha |
| June | — |
| July | — |
| August | Pramod |
| September | — |
| October | Ovi |
| November | — |
| December | Sumit |

stimuli.title: Six officers and their joining years
stimuli.content:
Six officers Vasudha, Waqar, Yamuna, Zeeshan, Aniket and Bhumika joined a bank in six different years among 2013, 2015, 2018, 2019, 2022 and 2024. Each works in a different department among Audit, Credit, HR, IT, Retail and Treasury.

- Vasudha joined in an even-numbered year and works in Credit.
- The person who works in HR joined exactly one year after Vasudha.
- Zeeshan works in HR.
- Aniket joined exactly nine years after Bhumika.
- The person who works in Treasury joined most recently.
- Yamuna joined after Zeeshan but before Aniket.
- The person who works in Audit joined earliest.
- Bhumika does not work in Retail.
stimuli.solution:
The only two listed years one year apart are 2018 and 2019, so Vasudha (even year, Credit) joined in 2018 and Zeeshan (HR) in 2019. Nine-year gaps: 2013–2022 and 2015–2024. If Bhumika = 2013 and Aniket = 2022, Yamuna must join after 2019 and before 2022, which no listed year allows. So Bhumika = 2015, Aniket = 2024 (Treasury, the latest year), Yamuna = 2022 and Waqar = 2013 (Audit, the earliest). IT and Retail remain for Bhumika and Yamuna; Bhumika is not in Retail, so Bhumika = IT and Yamuna = Retail.

| Year | Officer | Department |
|---|---|---|
| 2013 | Waqar | Audit |
| 2015 | Bhumika | IT |
| 2018 | Vasudha | Credit |
| 2019 | Zeeshan | HR |
| 2022 | Yamuna | Retail |
| 2024 | Aniket | Treasury |

stimuli.title: Four coded sentences about metal prices
stimuli.content:
In a certain code language:
'gold price rises today' is written as 'mo ki ta ru'
'silver price falls today' is written as 'ki ne zo ru'
'demand rises for gold' is written as 'ta pa mo lu'
'silver demand is high' is written as 'zo pa vi sa'

(The codes of the words in a sentence may appear in any order.)
stimuli.solution: silver = zo (sentences 2 and 4); demand = pa (sentences 3 and 4); price and today share {ki, ru} (sentences 1 and 2) and cannot be told apart; gold and rises share {mo, ta} (sentences 1 and 3) and cannot be told apart. Then falls = ne (sentence 2), for = lu (sentence 3), and is and high share {vi, sa}.

stimuli.title: Machine: shortest word to the left
stimuli.content:
A word arrangement machine rearranges a line of words step by step. In each step it takes the word with the fewest letters among the words not yet arranged (if two such words have the same number of letters, the one that comes first in alphabetical order) and places it immediately to the right of the words already arranged (in Step I, at the extreme left). The other words keep their order. The machine stops when all the words are arranged.

stimuli.title: Machine: largest number to the right
stimuli.content:
A number arrangement machine rearranges a line of numbers step by step. In each step it takes the largest number among those not yet arranged and places it immediately to the left of the numbers already arranged at the right end (in Step I, at the extreme right). The other numbers keep their order. The machine stops when all the numbers are arranged.

stimuli.title: Machine: words lose a letter, numbers lose the word length
stimuli.content:
A word and number arrangement machine rearranges a line step by step. In each step it takes the word that comes first in alphabetical order among the words not yet arranged and the largest number not yet arranged. The word is written without its last letter, and the number is reduced by the number of letters in that word (counted before the letter is removed). The shortened word and then the reduced number are placed immediately to the right of the elements already arranged (in Step I, at the extreme left). All other elements keep their order. The machine stops when every element has been arranged.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Some persons sit in a row, all facing north. Ritu sits 12th from the left end and Sohail sits 8th from the right end. Exactly three persons sit between Ritu and Sohail. What is the minimum possible number of persons in the row?

solution.concept: Two cases: the two persons may or may not 'cross' each other
solution.explanation: Sohail is either to the right of Ritu or to her left. Right: Sohail is 16th from the left and 8th from the right, so the row has 16 + 8 − 1 = 23 persons. Left: Sohail is 12 − 4 = 8th from the left and 8th from the right, so the row has 8 + 8 − 1 = 15 persons. The minimum is 15.
steps: Case 1, Sohail to the right of Ritu: Sohail = 12 + 4 = 16th from the left → total 16 + 8 − 1 = 23
Case 2, Sohail to the left of Ritu: Sohail = 12 − 4 = 8th from the left → total 8 + 8 − 1 = 15
Check case 2: Ritu at 12 of 15 is 4th from the right, and seats 9–11 lie between them: valid
Minimum = 15
solution.why_others_wrong: 23 is the maximum (the non-crossing case); 19 and 17 come from adding ranks without the between-count.

Ojas sits third to the left of Nisha, and only one person sits between Ojas and the east end of the row. How many persons sit to the left of Mohan?

solution.concept: Facing south: the left is towards the east
solution.explanation: Count seats from the west end. Mohan = 4. Nisha is six seats away: 4 + 6 = 10 (4 − 6 is impossible). Facing south, Ojas's seat three to Nisha's left is to the east: 13. One person sits between Ojas and the east end, so the row has 14 persons. Mohan's left is towards the east, where seats 5 to 14 hold 10 persons.
steps: Mohan = 4th from the west
Nisha = 4 + 6 = 10 (five persons between)
Ojas = 10 + 3 = 13 (left of a south-facing person = east)
One person between Ojas and the east end ⇒ 14 persons
Persons to Mohan's left (east of seat 4) = 14 − 4 = 10
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 counts the persons to Mohan's west, which is his right; 9 and 11 are off-by-one counts.

Five persons Aisha, Balraj, Chitra, Dev and Elina live on the five floors of a building, one on each floor. The lowermost floor is numbered 1 and the topmost floor 5.
- Chitra lives on an even-numbered floor.
- Only one person lives between Chitra and Aisha.
- Balraj lives immediately above Chitra.
- Dev lives on a floor below Aisha's floor.
- Elina does not live on the topmost floor.

Who lives on the floor immediately below Chitra?

solution.concept: Floor puzzle: test the cases of the most restricted person
solution.explanation: Chitra is on floor 2 or 4. If she were on 2, Balraj would be on 3, Aisha on 4, Dev on 1 and Elina on the top floor, which is not allowed. So Chitra is on 4, Balraj on 5, Aisha on 2, Dev on 1 and Elina on 3. Elina lives immediately below Chitra.
steps: Case Chitra = 2: Balraj 3, Aisha 4, Dev 1 → Elina 5 (top): rejected
Case Chitra = 4: Balraj 5, Aisha 2 (6 does not exist), Dev 1, Elina 3
Floor 3 (below Chitra): Elina
solution.why_others_wrong: Balraj lives above Chitra; Aisha and Dev are on floors 2 and 1.

Four persons Garima, Hamid, Ishani and Jeevan live on the four floors of a building, one on each floor (floor 1 is the lowermost). Each of them likes a different drink among Coffee, Juice, Milk and Tea.
- The person who likes Coffee lives on the topmost floor.
- Garima lives immediately below the person who likes Coffee.
- Ishani lives on a floor above Jeevan's floor.
- Hamid lives on a floor below Jeevan's floor.
- The person who likes Tea lives immediately above the person who likes Milk.
- Jeevan does not like Milk.

Which drink does Garima like?

solution.concept: Floor plus one attribute
solution.explanation: Coffee is on floor 4 and Garima on floor 3. Ishani is above Jeevan and Jeevan above Hamid, so Ishani = 4, Jeevan = 2 and Hamid = 1. Tea is immediately above Milk: floors 2–1 or 3–2. If Tea were on 3, Milk would be on 2 (Jeevan), which is not allowed. So Tea = 2 (Jeevan), Milk = 1 (Hamid) and Juice = 3 (Garima).
steps: Coffee = floor 4, Garima = floor 3
Hamid < Jeevan < Ishani ⇒ Hamid 1, Jeevan 2, Ishani 4
Tea–Milk on (3, 2) would give Jeevan Milk: rejected ⇒ Tea 2, Milk 1
Garima (floor 3) likes Juice

solution.explanation: Kiran's father's father has only one son, and Kiran's father is a son of his, so that only son is Kiran's own father. The girl is the daughter of Kiran's father: Kiran's sister.
steps: My father's father = Kiran's paternal grandfather
His only son = Kiran's father
Daughter of Kiran's father = Kiran's sister
solution.why_others_wrong: Cousin would need the 'only son' to be a different man (an uncle), which 'only' rules out.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Decoding a chain that crosses to a sibling's family
solution.explanation: P is the daughter of Q, and Q is the wife of R, so R is P's father. R is the brother of S, so S is P's aunt. S is the mother of T, so T is the child of P's father's sister: P's cousin.
steps: P % Q: P is Q's daughter
Q * R: Q is R's wife ⇒ R is P's father
R $ S: R is S's brother ⇒ S is P's aunt
S # T: S is T's mother ⇒ T is P's cousin
solution.why_others_wrong: Sister would need T to share P's parents; niece is T's relation to R; aunt is S's relation to P.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A family of three generations has eight members: Arvind, Bimla, Chetan, Deepti, Eshaan, Falguni, Girish and Harleen. Arvind, Chetan, Eshaan and Girish are male; the others are female. There are three married couples.
- Eshaan is the only grandson of Bimla.
- Falguni is the daughter of Girish.
- Harleen is the daughter-in-law of Arvind.
- Deepti is the sister-in-law of Harleen.
- Girish is the son-in-law of Bimla.
- Chetan is the father of Eshaan.
- Arvind and Bimla are married to each other and have only two children.

How is Girish related to Eshaan?

solution.concept: Building a three-generation tree from in-law clues
solution.explanation: Arvind and Bimla have two children: Harleen is married to their son and Girish to their daughter. Chetan, a male, is Eshaan's father and must be the son (Girish is the son-in-law), so Chetan's wife is Harleen. Deepti, female and Harleen's sister-in-law, is the daughter, married to Girish; Falguni is their daughter. Girish is the husband of Eshaan's father's sister: Eshaan's uncle.
steps: Generation 1: Arvind + Bimla, two children: one son (husband of Harleen), one daughter (wife of Girish)
Chetan (male, father of Eshaan) = the son, married to Harleen
Deepti (female) = the daughter, married to Girish; Falguni = their daughter
Girish = husband of Eshaan's paternal aunt ⇒ uncle
solution.why_others_wrong: Brother-in-law is Girish's relation to Chetan; father-in-law and grandfather belong to generation 1.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Meena walks 15 m towards the west. She then turns right and walks 8 m. How far is she from her starting point, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Displacement with an 8-15-17 triangle
solution.explanation: Turning right from west means facing north. She is 15 m west and 8 m north of the start: √(225 + 64) = 17 m, towards the north-west.
steps: Right from west = north; 8 m → (−15, 8)
√(15² + 8²) = 17 m; west and north → North-West
solution.why_others_wrong: 23 m adds the two legs; North-East reverses the east–west direction.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Point P is 6 m north of point Q. Point R is 6 m west of point Q. Point S is 6 m south of point R. In which direction is point P with respect to point S?

solution.concept: Placing points on a grid
solution.explanation: With Q at (0, 0): P = (0, 6), R = (−6, 0), S = (−6, −6). From S to P is 6 m east and 12 m north, so P is to the north-east of S.
steps: P − S = (6, 12): east and north ⇒ North-East
solution.why_others_wrong: South-East and North-West mix up the signs; North ignores the 6 m east component.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: One evening before sunset, Ravi was standing in an open field. His shadow fell exactly behind him. Which direction was he facing?

solution.concept: Shadows in the evening
solution.explanation: In the evening the sun is in the west, so shadows fall towards the east. The shadow is behind Ravi, so his back is to the east and he faces west (towards the sun).
steps: Evening sun → west; shadow → east
Shadow behind him ⇒ his back faces east
So he faces West
solution.why_others_wrong: East is where the shadow points, not where he faces.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: A girl is facing east. She turns 90° clockwise, then 180° clockwise, and then 45° anticlockwise. Which direction is she facing now?

solution.concept: Net rotation
solution.explanation: Measure directions clockwise from north: east = 90°. 90 + 90 = 180° (south), + 180 = 360° (north), − 45 = 315°, which is north-west.
steps: East = 90°
−45° → 315° (north-west)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Asha starts from her house and walks 5 km north. She turns right and walks 3 km, then turns right again and walks 5 km. How far is she from her house, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Legs that cancel out
solution.explanation: The 5 km north and 5 km south cancel; only the 3 km east remains. She is 3 km east of her house.
steps: 5 km north → (0, 5)
Right (east) 3 km → (3, 5)
Right (south) 5 km → (3, 0)
3 km, East
solution.why_others_wrong: 13 km adds every leg; West reverses the direction of the 3 km leg.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Village X is 12 km east of village Y. Village Z is 9 km south of village X. What is the shortest distance between villages Y and Z?

solution.concept: Pythagoras on a 9-12-15 triangle
solution.explanation: Y, X and Z form a right angle at X: YZ = √(12² + 9²) = √225 = 15 km.
solution.why_others_wrong: 21 km is the path through X, not the shortest distance.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Ankit and Bunty start from the same point. Ankit walks 7 km north, turns right and walks 4 km. Bunty walks 5 km south, turns right and walks 1 km. How far apart are they now, and in which direction is Ankit with respect to Bunty?

solution.concept: Two walkers: subtract the final positions
solution.explanation: Ankit ends at (4, 7). Bunty, turning right while facing south, faces west and ends at (−1, −5). Ankit − Bunty = (5, 12): 13 km, towards the north-east.
steps: Ankit: 7 north → (0, 7); right = east, 4 → (4, 7)
Bunty: 5 south → (0, −5); right of south = west, 1 → (−1, −5)
Difference (5, 12) → √(25 + 144) = 13 km; north and east → North-East
solution.why_others_wrong: South-West is Bunty's direction from Ankit; 17 km adds the legs (12 + 5).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: One morning after sunrise, Ishaan and Yatin were standing back to back. Ishaan's shadow fell exactly to his left. Which direction was Yatin facing?

solution.concept: Morning shadows with two observers
solution.explanation: In the morning the sun is in the east, so shadows fall to the west. Ishaan's left points west, so Ishaan faces north. Standing back to back, Yatin faces the opposite way: south.
steps: Morning sun → east; shadow → west
Ishaan's left = west ⇒ Ishaan faces north
Back to back ⇒ Yatin faces south
solution.why_others_wrong: North is Ishaan's direction, not Yatin's.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Point P is 10 m east of point Q. Point R is the midpoint of the line joining P and Q. Point S is 12 m north of point R. How far is point S from point Q, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Midpoints on a grid
solution.explanation: With Q at (0, 0), P = (10, 0), so R = (5, 0) and S = (5, 12). S is 5 m east and 12 m north of Q: 13 m, towards the north-east.
steps: S = R + 12 m north = (5, 12)
QS = √(25 + 144) = 13 m; North-East
solution.why_others_wrong: North-West reverses the east component; 12 m ignores it.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability

solution.concept: Coded directions converted to coordinates
solution.explanation: With K at (0, 0): J = (5, 0), L = (5, 9), M = (−3, 9), N = (−3, 6). N is 3 m west and 6 m north of K: √45 = 3√5 m, towards the north-west.
steps: N − K = (−3, 6) → √(9 + 36) = 3√5 m; west and north → North-West
solution.why_others_wrong: South-East is K's direction from N; √41 m uses the wrong north–south gap (5 m).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In which direction is point D with respect to point A?

solution.concept: Coordinates of a chain of points
solution.explanation: D − A = (11, 8): east and north, so D is to the north-east of A.
steps: D − A = (11, 8) → North-East

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the shortest distance between points A and C?

solution.concept: Pythagoras on a 6-8-10 triangle
solution.explanation: A is 6 m west of B and C is 8 m north of B, so AC = √(36 + 64) = 10 m.
solution.why_others_wrong: 14 m is the path through B.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which point lies on the straight line segment joining A and G?

solution.concept: Points with the same x-coordinate lie on one north–south line
solution.explanation: A = (−6, 0) and G = (−6, 8) lie on the same north–south line. F = (−6, 4) is on that line between them.
steps: Only F has x = −6 and 0 < y < 8
solution.why_others_wrong: B and E are east of the line; C is 6 m east of G.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Starting from point S, a car travels 20 km north, turns right and travels 15 km, turns right again and travels 27 km, and then turns left and travels 9 km. How far is the car from S, and in which direction?

solution.concept: Net displacement with a 7-24-25 triangle
solution.explanation: Net east: 15 + 9 = 24 km (turning left while facing south means facing east). Net south: 27 − 20 = 7 km. Distance = √(24² + 7²) = 25 km, towards the south-east.
steps: 20 km north → (0, 20)
Right (east) 15 → (15, 20)
Right (south) 27 → (15, −7)
Left of south = east, 9 → (24, −7)
√(576 + 49) = 25 km; east and south → South-East
solution.why_others_wrong: North-East forgets that the car ends 7 km south of S; 31 km adds the components.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code language, PLANET is written as QKBMFS. How is SILVER written in that code language?

solution.concept: Alternating forward and backward shifts
solution.explanation: PLANET → QKBMFS: P+1, L−1, A+1, N−1, E+1, T−1. The letters in odd places move one step forward and those in even places one step back. SILVER: S+1 = T, I−1 = H, L+1 = M, V−1 = U, E+1 = F, R−1 = Q.
steps: SILVER: S→T, I→H, L→M, V→U, E→F, R→Q
Code: THMUFQ
solution.why_others_wrong: TJMWFS shifts every letter forward; RHKUDQ shifts every letter back; THMUFS gets the last letter wrong.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'falls'?

solution.concept: Eliminating shared words
solution.explanation: Sentence 2 is 'silver price falls today'. silver = zo (common to sentences 2 and 4), and price and today take ki and ru (common to sentences 1 and 2). The code left is ne.
steps: Sentences 2 & 4: silver = zo
Sentences 1 & 2: {price, today} = {ki, ru}
Sentence 2: falls = ne

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'demand'?

solution.concept: Common word, common code
solution.explanation: 'demand' appears in sentences 3 and 4, and the only code common to both is pa.
steps: Sentence 3 codes: ta pa mo lu; sentence 4 codes: zo pa vi sa
Common code: pa ⇒ demand = pa

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which word is coded as 'lu'?

solution.concept: Decoding a code back to a word
solution.explanation: Sentence 3 is 'demand rises for gold' = 'ta pa mo lu'. demand = pa, and gold and rises take mo and ta (shared with sentence 1). So lu = for.
steps: demand = pa (sentences 3 & 4)
{gold, rises} = {mo, ta} (sentences 1 & 3)
Remaining: for = lu

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 'gold'?

solution.concept: When two words always appear together
solution.explanation: gold and rises appear together in sentences 1 and 3 and never apart, so they share the codes mo and ta in some order. The code for gold cannot be fixed.
steps: Sentences 1 & 3 share {gold, rises} and {mo, ta}
No sentence contains one without the other
So gold = mo or ta: cannot be determined
solution.why_others_wrong: mo and ta are each possible but neither is certain; ki belongs to price or today.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, MOTHER is written as PNIUSF. How is SECOND written in that code?

solution.concept: Swap each pair of letters, then shift forward
solution.explanation: MOTHER → split into pairs MO | TH | ER → swap each pair → OM HT RE → move each letter one step forward → PN IU SF. SECOND → SE | CO | ND → ES OC DN → FT PD EO = FTPDEO.
steps: Check: MOTHER → OMHTRE → +1 → PNIUSF
SECOND → ESOCDN
+1 → FTPDEO
solution.why_others_wrong: TFDPOE shifts without swapping; FTPDOE swaps only two pairs correctly; RDBNMC shifts backwards.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, MARKET is written as NSFBLU. How is PLANET written in that code?

solution.concept: Odd-place letters first, then even-place letters, then +1
solution.explanation: MARKET: letters in odd places (M, R, E) are written first, then those in even places (A, K, T): MREAKT; each letter then moves one step forward: NSFBLU. PLANET → P, A, E then L, N, T → PAELNT → QBFMOU.
steps: MARKET → MRE + AKT → +1 → NSF BLU (matches)
PLANET → PAE + LNT = PAELNT
+1 → QBFMOU
solution.why_others_wrong: QMBOFU shifts without rearranging; PAELNT rearranges without shifting; QBFOMU swaps two letters.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, CAKE is written as 19 and BOOK is written as 26. How is DESK written in that code?

solution.concept: Product of end-letter positions plus word length
solution.explanation: CAKE: C (3) × E (5) = 15, plus 4 letters = 19. BOOK: B (2) × K (11) = 22, plus 4 = 26. DESK: D (4) × K (11) = 44, plus 4 = 48.
steps: CAKE: 3 × 5 + 4 = 19 (matches)
BOOK: 2 × 11 + 4 = 26 (matches)
solution.why_others_wrong: 44 forgets to add the number of letters; 52 adds twice the number of letters; 26 is the code of BOOK.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, ACE is written as 27 and BED as 33. How is FACE written in that code?

solution.concept: Sum of positions multiplied by the number of letters
steps: ACE: 9 × 3 = 27; BED: 11 × 3 = 33 (both match)
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 is only the sum; 45 multiplies by 3 instead of the number of letters; 75 multiplies by 5.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: If 'sky' is called 'sea', 'sea' is called 'land', 'land' is called 'tree', 'tree' is called 'river' and 'river' is called 'cloud', then where do fish live?

solution.concept: Word substitution: answer with the new name of the real thing
solution.explanation: Fish live in the sea, and in this language the sea is called 'land'.
steps: Real answer: fish live in the sea
'sea' is called 'land'
Answer: land
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Sea' is the real word, not its code; 'River' is the code for tree; 'Cloud' is the code for river.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 47392?

solution.concept: Table coding with conditions on the end digits
solution.explanation: 4 and 2 are both even, so condition (ii) interchanges the codes of the end digits: 4 → # and 2 → @ swap places. The middle digits 7, 3, 9 are T, P, M.
steps: First digit 4 (even), last digit 2 (even): condition (ii)
Raw codes: # T P M @
Interchange ends: @TPM#
solution.why_others_wrong: #TPM@ ignores the condition; #TP$@ applies (iv); XTPMY applies (iii).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 58164?

solution.concept: Table coding with conditions on the end digits
solution.explanation: 5 is odd and 4 is even, so condition (i) codes both end digits as the code of 4 (#). The middle digits 8, 1, 6 are &, K, %.
steps: First 5 (odd), last 4 (even): condition (i)
Both ends → # (code of 4)
Code: #&K%#
solution.why_others_wrong: R&K%# is the raw code; R&K%R uses the first digit's code; #&K%R swaps the ends instead.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 82735?

solution.concept: Table coding with conditions on the end digits
solution.explanation: 8 is even and 5 is odd, so condition (iii) applies: the first digit becomes X and the last Y. The middle digits 2, 7, 3 are @, T, P.
steps: First 8 (even), last 5 (odd): condition (iii)
Middle: 2 → @, 7 → T, 3 → P
Code: X@TPY
solution.why_others_wrong: &@TPR is the raw code; R@TP& interchanges the ends (condition ii); &@$PR applies (iv).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: What is the code for 39517?

solution.concept: Table coding with conditions on the end digits
solution.explanation: 3 and 7 are both odd, so condition (iv) applies: only the third digit (5) changes, to $. The code is P M $ K T.
steps: First 3 (odd), last 7 (odd): condition (iv)
Third digit 5 → $
Code: PM$KT
solution.why_others_wrong: PMRKT is the raw code; TMRKP interchanges the ends; XMRKY applies condition (iii).

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, GARDEN is written as AGKIXT. The letters in odd places (1st, 3rd, 5th) are moved two places forward in the alphabet, the letters in even places are moved three places back, and then the two halves of the result are interchanged. How is SILVER written in that code?

solution.concept: Position-dependent shifts followed by a half swap
solution.explanation: SILVER: S+2 = U, I−3 = F, L+2 = N, V−3 = S, E+2 = G, R−3 = O → UFNSGO. Interchanging the halves (UFN | SGO) gives SGOUFN.
steps: Check GARDEN: G+2 I, A−3 X, R+2 T, D−3 A, E+2 G, N−3 K → IXT AGK → AGKIXT (matches)
SILVER → U F N S G O
Swap halves → SGOUFN
solution.why_others_wrong: UFNSGO skips the half swap; SGONFU reverses the second half; UFTSGO mis-shifts L.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In a certain code, BANK is written as 26 and LOAN is written as 10. Using the same rule, how is CREDIT written?

solution.concept: Consonant total minus vowel total
solution.explanation: BANK: consonants B (2) + N (14) + K (11) = 27, vowel A (1); 27 − 1 = 26. LOAN: L (12) + N (14) = 26, vowels O (15) + A (1) = 16; 26 − 16 = 10. CREDIT: consonants C 3 + R 18 + D 4 + T 20 = 45; vowels E 5 + I 9 = 14; 45 − 14 = 31.
steps: CREDIT consonants: 3 + 18 + 4 + 20 = 45
CREDIT vowels: 5 + 9 = 14
solution.why_others_wrong: 59 adds all six positions; 45 is the consonant total alone; 14 is the vowel total.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
In a certain code language:
'fund flow is strong' is written as 've ko ri ta',
'strong rupee flow' is written as 'ta mu ko',
'rupee is weak' is written as 'mu ri zi', and
'weak fund outlook' is written as 'zi ve pa'.
(The codes of the words in a sentence may appear in any order.)

What is the code for 'fund is'?

solution.concept: Chained elimination across four sentences
solution.explanation: {strong, flow} = {ta, ko} (sentences 1 and 2), so rupee = mu (sentence 2). Then from sentence 3, rupee = mu leaves {is, weak} = {ri, zi}; weak also appears in sentence 4, whose codes include zi but not ri, so weak = zi and is = ri. From sentence 1 the code left for fund is ve.
steps: Sentences 1 & 2: {strong, flow} = {ta, ko} ⇒ rupee = mu
Sentences 3 & 4 share weak and zi ⇒ weak = zi
Sentence 3: is = ri
Sentence 1: fund = ve
fund is = ve ri
solution.why_others_wrong: ko belongs to strong or flow; zi is weak; ta belongs to strong or flow.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

K 7 @ B 3 E # 9 M U 4 $ R 2 % A 8 T & 6 Q

Which element is exactly midway between the 7th element from the left end and the 5th element from the right end?

solution.concept: Converting a right-end position before finding the midpoint
solution.explanation: The series has 21 elements, so the 5th from the right is the 17th from the left. Midway between positions 7 and 17 is position 12: $.
steps: Total elements = 21
5th from the right = 21 − 5 + 1 = 17th from the left
Midpoint of 7 and 17 = 12
12th element = $
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 and R are the 11th and 13th elements (off by one); U is the 10th.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Study the following arrangement of letters, numbers and symbols and answer the question.

5 G @ 3 K 8 E # 2 W 7 $ L 4 I 9 % P 6 & N 1 Y

What is the sum of all the numbers in the arrangement each of which is immediately followed by a consonant?

solution.explanation: Numbers immediately followed by a consonant: 5 G; 3 K; 2 W; 1 Y. Their sum is 5 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 11.
steps: Check each number and the element after it
Discard those followed by a vowel (8 E, 4 I) or a symbol (7 $, 9 %, 6 &)
Qualifying: 5, 3, 2, 1
Sum = 11

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which letter is 5th to the right of the 12th letter from the right end of the English alphabet?

solution.concept: Converting a right-end position
solution.explanation: The 12th letter from the right is the (27 − 12) = 15th from the left, O. Five places to its right is the 20th letter: T.
steps: 12th from the right = 15th from the left = O
20th letter = T
solution.why_others_wrong: J is 5th to the left of O; U and S are off by one.

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following words can be formed using the letters of the word 'DEPARTMENT' (each letter used no more often than it appears in DEPARTMENT)?

solution.concept: Checking letters against the source word

MASTER needs S (absent)

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many pairs of letters are there in the word 'MOBILE' each of which has as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet (counting both forward and backward)?

solution.concept: Comparing word gaps with alphabet gaps
solution.explanation: Pairs found: OL, BE. Total 2.

For each pair, compare the gap in the word with the gap in the alphabet
Matching pairs: O–L, B–E

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: How many letters are there between the 6th letter from the left end and the 9th letter from the right end of the English alphabet?

solution.concept: Counting letters between two positions
solution.explanation: The 6th letter from the left is F (6). The 9th from the right is the 18th from the left, R. Between positions 6 and 18 there are 18 − 6 − 1 = 11 letters.
steps: 6th from left = F
9th from right = 27 − 9 = 18th = R
Between: 11

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the word 'GRAPHIC', each consonant is replaced by the letter immediately after it in the English alphabet and each vowel by the letter immediately before it. How many letters appear more than once in the new letter group?

solution.concept: Transform, then look for repeats
solution.explanation: G→H, R→S, A→Z, P→Q, H→I, I→H, C→D gives H S Z Q I H D. Only H appears twice.
steps: Consonants +1: G→H, R→S, P→Q, H→I, C→D
Vowels −1: A→Z, I→H
New group: HSZQIHD
Repeated: H only
solution.why_others_wrong: 'None' misses that H (from G) and H (from I) coincide.

questions.question_text: How many pairs of letters are there in the word 'BACKGROUND' each of which has as many letters between them in the word as in the English alphabet (counting both forward and backward)?

solution.explanation: Pairs found: BA. Total 1.

Matching pairs: B–A

Compare place by place
Unchanged: none

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: In the word 'COMPUTERS', each letter in an odd place (1st, 3rd, …) is replaced by the next letter of the English alphabet and each letter in an even place by the previous letter. The new letters are then arranged in reverse alphabetical order (Z to A) from left to right. Which letter will be 4th from the left?

solution.concept: Transform, sort in reverse, count
solution.explanation: New letters: D N N O V S F Q T. In reverse alphabetical order: V T S Q O N N F D. The 4th from the left is Q.
steps: Odd places +1, even places −1: C→D O→N M→N P→O U→V T→S E→F R→Q S→T
Reverse order: V T S Q O N N F D
4th from the left: Q

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text: Which of the following words CANNOT be formed using the letters of the word 'ASSOCIATION' (each letter used no more often than it appears in ASSOCIATION)?

questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: The state has made it mandatory for every new building with a built-up area above 500 square metres to install a rainwater-harvesting system. A newly built office building of 800 square metres in the state has no such system.

Conclusions:
I. The rule is not being enforced anywhere in the state.
II. The new office building does not comply with the rule.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: The building is new and above 500 square metres, so the rule applies; without the system it does not comply (II). One building's failure does not show that the rule is ignored everywhere (I fails).
steps: Rule applies: new building, 800 > 500 square metres
No system ⇒ non-compliance: II follows
A single case cannot establish that enforcement fails everywhere: I does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I and Both generalise from one building to the whole state.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Only conclusion II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: Tomato prices in the city doubled in July after heavy rain damaged the crop in the neighbouring districts.

Conclusions:
I. Tomato prices in the city will fall in August.
II. Tomatoes sold in the city come only from the neighbouring districts.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: I is a prediction about August that the statement does not support. The rain-hit districts clearly supply some of the city's tomatoes, but 'only' goes beyond what is stated (II fails).
steps: I: a forecast; nothing in the statement fixes August prices: does not follow
II: the statement shows the neighbouring districts matter, not that they are the sole source: does not follow
solution.why_others_wrong: Only II is the trap: the price jump suggests the districts are an important source, not the only one.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Neither conclusion I nor II follows

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Read the statement and the two conclusions. Assume everything in the statement to be true, and decide which conclusion(s) logically follow from it.

Statement: All five members of the audit team are chartered accountants. Exactly two of the five also hold an MBA. Priya is a member of the audit team and does not hold an MBA.

Conclusions:
I. Priya is a chartered accountant.
II. Three members of the audit team do not hold an MBA.

options.text: Neither conclusion I nor II follows
Both conclusions I and II follow

solution.concept: A conclusion must follow from the statement alone
solution.explanation: Every member is a chartered accountant, and Priya is a member, so I follows. Exactly two of five hold an MBA, so the other three do not, so II follows.
steps: All members are CAs; Priya is a member ⇒ I follows
5 − 2 = 3 members without an MBA ⇒ II follows
solution.why_others_wrong: Only I misses the arithmetic in 'exactly two of the five'; Only II misses the direct application to Priya.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both conclusions I and II follow

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. The state government announced a 50% cut in bus fares for students from 1 June.
II. The number of students travelling by state buses rose sharply in June.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Cheaper fares make the bus more attractive to students, and the rise came in the month the cut began. I explains II, so I is the cause and II its effect.
steps: I (fare cut from 1 June) comes first
Lower fares → more student passengers in June: I explains II
So I is the cause, II the effect
solution.why_others_wrong: II cannot cause I (the cut was announced before the rise); a common cause or independent causes would ignore the direct link.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. Several flights at the city airport were cancelled on Tuesday morning.
II. Dense fog reduced visibility at the city airport to under 50 metres on Tuesday morning.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Very low visibility makes take-offs and landings unsafe, which leads airlines to cancel flights. II explains I, so II is the cause and I its effect.
steps: II: fog, visibility under 50 m
I: cancellations the same morning
Fog → unsafe flying → cancellations: II is the cause
solution.why_others_wrong: Cancelled flights cannot create fog, so A is impossible; E would need a third event behind both, but the fog itself explains the cancellations.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. All the hotels in the hill town reported full occupancy last weekend.
II. Traffic jams stretched for several kilometres on the road to the hill town last weekend.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Full hotels do not cause traffic on the approach road, and the jams do not fill hotels. Both are what a single event, a surge of tourists (for example over a long holiday weekend), would produce. So both are effects of a common cause.
steps: No direct causal link either way
Both are typical results of one trigger: a rush of visitors
So both are effects of a common cause
solution.why_others_wrong: Effects of independent causes would need two unrelated reasons that happened to coincide on the same weekend; one tourist rush explains both more simply.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. The retail price of onions in the city has risen by 30% this month.
II. The city's municipal corporation has raised property tax rates for the coming year.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Each statement is an outcome: onion prices respond to supply and crop conditions, and the tax rise to the corporation's budget needs. Neither explains the other, and no single event explains both. They are effects of independent causes.
steps: I is an effect of market supply conditions
II is an effect of the corporation's revenue decisions
No link and no shared trigger ⇒ effects of independent causes
solution.why_others_wrong: A common cause would need one event driving both a vegetable price and a civic tax decision; nothing suggests one.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. The school has decided to keep its playground open to local children on Sundays.
II. Parents in the locality complained that their children had no safe place to play on weekends.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: The parents' complaint (II) is the problem; opening the playground on Sundays (I) is the school's response to it. II is the cause and I its effect.
steps: II reports a need: no safe place to play on weekends
I meets that need directly
So II is the cause and I the effect
solution.why_others_wrong: I cannot cause II (the decision would end the complaint, not create it); treating them as unrelated ignores the obvious response.
solution.final_answer: Option B: Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes or of a common cause, or one may be the effect of the other. Decide the relationship.

I. Many residents of the coastal district were moved to relief camps on Thursday.
II. All schools in the coastal district remained closed from Thursday to Saturday.

options.text: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

solution.concept: Cause and effect: look for a direct link, a shared trigger, or none
solution.explanation: Moving residents does not close schools, and closing schools does not move residents. Both are standard precautions taken together after one trigger, such as a cyclone warning for the coast. So both are effects of a common cause.
steps: No direct link between evacuation and school closure
Both match the response to one emergency warning
So both are effects of a common cause
solution.why_others_wrong: A is tempting (schools are sometimes used as relief camps), but even then the closure would follow from the same emergency, not from the evacuation itself.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Statement: On the first working day of every month, when pensions are credited, many pensioners wait for over an hour at a bank branch.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action for the bank?

options.text: Stop crediting pensions on the first working day of the month
Ask pensioners to visit the branch only once a year
Keep the branch closed on the first working day of every month
Open extra counters and issue tokens to pensioners on the first few working days of every month

solution.concept: A course of action should solve the stated problem practically
solution.explanation: The problem is a predictable rush on known days. Extra counters and tokens on those days cut the waiting time directly without harming anyone.
steps: Problem: long waits on pension days
Cause: many pensioners come on the same days
Remedy: more service capacity on exactly those days
solution.why_others_wrong: Delaying pensions or closing the branch hurts the pensioners; asking them to come once a year is impractical and does not reduce the queue on the busy days.
solution.final_answer: Option D: Open extra counters and issue tokens to pensioners on the first few working days of every month

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
A survey of 500 customers of a bank found that 70% of the customers who use the bank's mobile app visited a branch at least once last month, while 90% of the customers who do not use the app visited a branch at least once last month.

Which of the following can be inferred from the survey?

options.text: Using the mobile app makes customers stop visiting branches
Most of the 500 surveyed customers use the mobile app
Among the surveyed customers, app users were less likely than non-users to have visited a branch last month
The bank should close some of its branches

solution.concept: Inference: state only what the figures show
solution.explanation: 70% of app users versus 90% of non-users visited a branch, so within the survey app users were less likely to visit. That is a direct reading of the figures.
steps: App users: 70% visited; non-users: 90% visited
70% < 90% ⇒ app users less likely to visit (within the survey)
No causal claim, split of users or recommendation can be drawn
solution.why_others_wrong: The survey shows an association, not that the app causes fewer visits (and 70% still visited); the split between users and non-users is never given; closing branches is a recommendation, not an inference.
solution.final_answer: Option C: Among the surveyed customers, app users were less likely than non-users to have visited a branch last month

questions.subject: Reasoning Ability
questions.question_text:
Argument: Six months after the city began charging cars a fee to enter the central business district during peak hours, the average speed of traffic in the district rose by 20%. So the entry fee has reduced congestion in the district.

Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

options.text: The number of metro passengers travelling to the district rose during the six months
Many drivers complained that the entry fee is too high
The fee applies only during peak hours on working days
During the same six months, a new ring road opened that lets vehicles crossing the city bypass the central business district altogether

solution.concept: Weakening a causal claim: offer another cause for the same effect
solution.explanation: The argument credits the fee for faster traffic. If a new ring road took through-traffic out of the district in the same period, the faster speeds may be due to the road, not the fee, so the conclusion is undermined.
steps: Conclusion: fee → faster traffic
A weakener supplies an alternative explanation for the same result
A new bypass road in the same period is such an explanation
solution.why_others_wrong: More metro passengers fits the argument (drivers switching to the metro); complaints about the price do not touch the effect on traffic; the peak-hour limit only describes the fee.
solution.final_answer: Option D: During the same six months, a new ring road opened that lets vehicles crossing the city bypass the central business district altogether
